title: 2 Rooks VS Queen!
summary: Coordinate the rooks with a king waiting move rather than rushing a ladder check.

nodes.question: How can two rooks overcome a queen and pawn?
nodes.explanation: The black queen and h7 pawn restrict their own king. White must coordinate the rooks while keeping its king safe from useful queen checks.

branches.title: Close the corner, then remove the queen blocker
commentary: Begin from the complete six-piece source diagram.
Rg1 controls the g-file and restricts the black king’s routes.
Kh8 is the source’s corner retreat.
Kb7 prepares the a-file rook’s eighth-rank attack while limiting useful nearby queen checks.
Qe6 is an independently selected representative queen move to test the mating idea.
Ra8+ checks along the eighth rank. This representative line still permits a queen interposition.
Qg8 interposes on the checking line, sacrificing the queen.
Rxg8# captures the blocker. The rook on g1 protects g8, while h7 blocks the black king’s remaining flight.
branches.classification: selected source idea with independent alternative queen defense and mating completion
branches.explanation: Rxg8# captures the blocker. The rook on g1 protects g8, while h7 blocks the black king’s remaining flight.

branches.title: Use the king tempo in the rook net
commentary: Compare the source’s retreat toward f8 rather than h8.
Rg1 establishes the g-file restriction.
Kf8 tries to escape toward the center before the mating net is complete.
Rf1+ checks on the f-file and denies the king its route down that file.
Kg8 retreats from the checking rook.
Rg2+ checks on the g-file, coordinating the second rook with Rf1.
Kh8 returns to the corner, where the h-pawn restricts its flight.
Kc7 is the source’s waiting move, leaving Black to disturb its defensive arrangement.
Qe6 is an independent representative defense, moving away from the diagonal that guarded f8.
Rf8+ reaches the mating rank with the other rook protecting the g-file.
Qg8 is an independently supplied interposition rather than an immediate mate declaration.
Rxg8# removes the queen blocker. Rg2 protects g8, and h7 prevents the king escaping down the h-file.
branches.classification: selected source idea with independent alternative queen defense and mating completion
branches.explanation: Rxg8# removes the queen blocker. Rg2 protects g8, and h7 prevents the king escaping down the h-file.

branches.title: Give an unsupported rook check
commentary: This independent comparison tests a premature checking attempt.
Rg1 preserves White’s win with correct coordination.
Kf8 is the source’s central retreat.
Rg8+ gives away the win by placing the rook next to the king without protection from Ra2 or Kb8.
Kxg8 collects that rook. The exact position is winning for Black; giving check does not compensate for the loose rook.
branches.classification: independent alternative with representative legal replies
branches.explanation: Kxg8 collects that rook. The exact position is winning for Black; giving check does not compensate for the loose rook.

exercises.answer: An unprotected rook on g8 can simply be captured. The winning nets keep a rook on the g-file to protect the other rook’s final capture.

exercises.prompt: Why does a king move help a rook attack?
exercises.answer: Kb7 or Kc7 maintains the rook threats while passing the move to Black. A queen move can leave the key checking rank or diagonal unguarded.
